lesson.title: Turning Impedance Upside Down: Admittance for Parallel AC Circuits
lesson.summary: Admittance Y = 1/Z, measured in siemens, restates a circuit's response to AC in a form that adds directly for parallel elements, mirroring how conductance simplifies parallel DC resistors.
lesson.body:
When resistors sit in parallel in a DC circuit, there is a shortcut that avoids the awkward reciprocal-of-a-sum formula: convert each resistance to a conductance, G = 1/R, and simply add the conductances, since Gtotal = G1 + G2 + ... for parallel branches. AC circuits have the same awkwardness with impedances in parallel, and the same shortcut works if we define admittance, Y = 1/Z, measured in siemens. Just as conductance is the reciprocal of resistance, admittance is the reciprocal of impedance, and parallel admittances add directly: Ytotal = Y1 + Y2 + ...

Admittance is complex, written Y = G + jB, where G is conductance, the real part, and B is susceptance, the imaginary part, covered next. Converting from Z = R + jX to Y requires multiplying by the complex conjugate to clear the imaginary part from the denominator: Y = 1/Z = (R - jX) / (R^2 + X^2). That means G = R / (R^2 + X^2) and B = -X / (R^2 + X^2). Here is the subtlety worth pausing on: G is not simply 1/R once reactance is present. The conductance of an RL or RC branch depends on both R and X together, and only collapses to 1/R when X = 0.

Return to the series RL impedance from before, Z = 30 + j40 ohms, which in polar form is 50 ohms at an angle of 53.13 degrees. Its admittance is Y = 1/Z. In polar form this inverts cleanly: Y = (1/50) at an angle of -53.13 degrees = 0.02 S at -53.13 degrees. Converting to rectangular form, Y = 0.02(cos 53.13 - j sin 53.13) = 0.02(0.6 - j0.8) = 0.012 - j0.016 siemens. Check this against the direct formula: G = 30/(30^2+40^2) = 30/2500 = 0.012 S, and B = -40/2500 = -0.016 S. Both routes agree. Notice the sign flip: an inductive impedance, positive X, produces a negative susceptance.

Admittance magnitude answers a simple physical question: for a given RMS voltage across a branch, how much current does it let through? A branch with large |Y| is an easy path for current; one with small |Y| is a hard path. This becomes especially valuable once several branches sit in parallel, since you can add their admittances directly, find the total current from I = VY, and only convert back to impedance at the end if you need it.

To see the payoff, put that RL branch, Y1 = 0.012 - j0.016 S, in parallel with a second, purely resistive branch, R2 = 25 ohms, so Y2 = 1/25 = 0.04 S with no imaginary part. Adding admittances directly gives Ytotal = Y1 + Y2 = 0.052 - j0.016 S. In polar form that is about 0.0544 S at an angle of -17.1 degrees, so the equivalent impedance is Ztotal = 1/Ytotal, about 17.6 + j5.4 ohms, magnitude about 18.4 ohms. Notice how much simpler that direct addition was than combining Z1 = 30 + j40 ohms and Z2 = 25 ohms with the reciprocal-of-a-sum impedance formula; the admittance route just adds two complex numbers and inverts once, at the very end. That conversion step, and the physical meaning of the imaginary part B on its own, is exactly where susceptance picks up the story.
